newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S.-China talks open with Beijing warning on Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-China talks open with Beijing warning on Taiwan.

text.p: China opened Sino-American talks on Wednesday with a demand for an end to "massive" U.S. arms sales to Taiwan and a warning that failure to manage tensions over the island would cause more disruptions in bilateral ties.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, by contrast, played down differences with Beijing and stressed President Bill Clinton's anxiousness to take positive steps in the relationship.

In an inauspicious beginning to talks Washington considers key to ensuring Sino-American ties are on the mend, Christopher was nearly 30 minutes late for his first meeting, with Foreign Minister Qian Qichen.

But his spokesman dismissed the delay as "not a big deal" because the Chinese were informed in advance that Christopher would be late so he could hold a last-minute consultation by telephone with officials travelling with Clinton in Australia.
Christopher's visit is his first to Beijing since a disastrous trip in 1994. He and Qian are setting the stage for talks in Manila on Sunday between Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
"The question of Taiwan is the core issue of Sino-American relations," Qian told a news conference with Christopher at the start of talks that will include meetings with Jiang and Premier Li Peng.
"If well-handled then the Sino-U.S relationship can grow smoothly. If mishandled, then our bilateral relationship will be subject to disruptions," he said.
"We attach importance to the commitments made by the U.S. government on the question of Taiwan. But we pay more attention to their action," he added.
Asked how Washington could promote stability across the Taiwan Strait, Qian referred to the 1982 Sino-U.S. communique pledging eventual termination of American arms sales to Taiwan.
"We can only feel reassured when this promise is turned into reality," Qian said.
The United States has made much of its concerns about China's willingness to sell nuclear technology and advanced conventional weapons to Iran and missiles to Pakistan.
Christopher said en route to Beijing he would again urge China to end nuclear cooperation with Iran and other officials said concerns about missiles transfers would also be discussed.
Qian used his opening statement at the news conference to insist China was not engaging in nuclear proliferation and in fact had stepped up efforts to control nuclear exports.

The United States has held up a 1985 agreement on peaceful nuclear cooperation because of concerns over Beijing's nuclear sales, although the two sides have recently begun talks aimed at allowing the accord to proceed. China is eager to buy billions of dollars worth of nuclear power reactors from U.S. firms.

Qian insisted China was upholding a 1994 commitment not to sell missiles to destabilising regions and said Beijing was more concerned "about massive sales by the United States of advanced weapons to Taiwan".

The United States insists its sale of "defensive" military equipment to Taiwan is consistent with the Taiwan Relations Act and the 1982 joint communique. It has provided Taiwan with millions of dollars worth of aircraft, ships and air-defence and anti-ship missiles.
The United States broke relations with Taiwan in 1979 and recognised communist China. But it maintains unofficial ties with the island.
China, which considers Taiwan a renegade province, remains extremely sensitive about U.S. dealings with the island.
Qian said Beijing was ready to speed talks on China's entry into the World Trade Organisation.

Christopher stressed that Clinton "recognises the enormous importance of China and the great potential of broader (bilateral) cooperation". The president "is anxious to take positive steps in this relationship", he said.
Both ministers said the relationship had improved.
